title: Fetal monitoring in labour: basics
summary: Intermittent auscultation vs continuous CTG, and recognising a fetal heart pattern that needs escalation.
redFlags: Fetal bradycardia, reduced variability, or late/variable/prolonged decelerations on CTG — escalate for prompt obstetric review.
Any abnormal fetal heart rate found on intermittent auscultation should prompt a switch to continuous CTG.

blocks.heading: Choosing the monitoring method
bullets: Intermittent auscultation is generally appropriate for women with a straightforward pregnancy and labour.

Continuous CTG is generally recommended where risk factors are present — for example meconium-stained liquor, maternal fever, an abnormal finding on auscultation, oxytocin use, or a higher-risk pregnancy — VERIFY the exact local risk-factor list, as it is set by local protocol and NICE intrapartum guidance.

blocks.heading: What to assess on a CTG
bullets: Baseline fetal heart rate, variability, presence of accelerations, and any decelerations and their pattern — this is a general assessment framework, not a substitute for formal CTG training.

VERIFY the current local classification system and terminology used for CTG interpretation before relying on any specific category label — fetal monitoring guidance and terminology have been revised over time, and older mnemonics taught previously may not match current local training.

blocks.heading: If a trace is concerning
bullets: Call for a senior review promptly rather than waiting to see if it resolves.
Simple measures while awaiting review can include a maternal position change, IV fluids, and stopping oxytocin if running — VERIFY local protocol for conservative measures.
Document clearly: time concern identified, actions taken, and time of senior review.
